title: Voltage Drop Calculations

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Parking lot at dusk, row of pole lights, a few noticeably dim at the far end. Matthew in the foreground. Medium shot.
scenes.says: Do the math before you drive out. If the calculation says the far end should be fine and your meter says otherwise, you've found a problem connection before anyone opens a pole. That's how you plan a voltage drop job: calculate first, then bring the right PPE, a CAT III or IV meter, and a plan for safe test points.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Cutaways: a long warehouse aisle, a corridor, a parking lot run. Matthew voice-over.
scenes.says: Every conductor has resistance, and current through it causes voltage drop. On long runs that can mean HID lamps that won't start, dimming problems, and wasted heat. LED drivers behave as constant power, so at lower voltage they draw more current, which makes the drop worse.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: NEC informational notes: 3% branch or feeder - 5% total
scenes.says: The NEC doesn't generally make voltage drop mandatory on ordinary branch circuits. Informational notes in Articles 210 and 215 recommend no more than 3 percent on a branch circuit or feeder, and 5 percent total. They're advisory, but specs, engineers and energy codes often make them mandatory on a project.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Whiteboard close-up as Matthew writes the formula and labels each symbol.
scenes.on_screen:
Single-phase: VD = (2 x K x I x L) / CM
Three-phase: VD = (1.732 x K x I x L) / CM
K = 12.9 copper, 21.2 aluminum - L = one-way feet
scenes.says: The single-phase formula, which covers 120 and 277 volt lighting circuits: VD equals 2 times K times I times L, divided by circular mils. K is about 12.9 for copper and 21.2 for aluminum. L is the one-way length; the 2 covers the return path. For balanced three-phase, use 1.732 instead of 2. Circular mils come from NEC Chapter 9, Table 8.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Whiteboard: worked example written step by step.
scenes.says: Worked example. A 277 volt parking-lot circuit, 12 amps, farthest pole 250 feet, 12 AWG copper. Two times 12.9 times 12 times 250 is 77,400. Divide by 6,530: 11.85 volts, or 4.3 percent. That's over 3. Try 10 AWG: 77,400 divided by 10,380 is 7.46 volts, 2.7 percent. Within 3.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew at the whiteboard, medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Upsizing affects terminals, box and conduit fill, and the EGC (NEC 250.122(B))
scenes.says: That calculation assumes all the load at the far end, so it's conservative. Before you promise a fix, remember that bigger conductors may need larger terminals, boxes and raceways. And upsizing for voltage drop generally means increasing the equipment grounding conductor proportionally, under 250.122(B).

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Site: senior tech in PPE measures line-to-neutral at the panel breaker with lights on, then at the last pole using leads installed earlier while locked out. Presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: 1 Calculate  2 PPE + CAT III/IV meter  3 Lights on, measure at panel  4 Measure at far luminaire via safe test points  5 Compare
scenes.says: In the field, calculate first, then risk assessment and PPE. With the lights on and stable, measure line-to-neutral at the panel breaker. At the farthest luminaire, measure only through accessible test points, or with leads installed while the fixture was de-energized, before power was restored. Subtract to get the measured drop and compare.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of a corroded splice in a pole base (de-energized, lock visible at the panel).
scenes.on_screen: Never strip or pierce insulation on live conductors to take a reading.
scenes.says: If measured drop is much higher than calculated, suspect a high-resistance connection: a loose or corroded splice, a failing wire nut, damaged wire. Measure at intermediate points to find it, then repair under LOTO. And never strip or pierce insulation on live conductors to get a reading. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Whiteboard numbers must match the lesson exactly (77,400; 6,530; 11.85 V; 4.3%; 10,380; 7.46 V; 2.7%). Site measurement performed by a qualified senior technician in PPE with a CAT III/IV meter; far-end leads shown being installed with the circuit locked out and verified dead before power is restored. No customer signage in the parking lot.
